title: A Century Ago, the House of Saud Seized Mecca and Medina
excerpt: How Abdulaziz ibn Saud's 1924–1925 conquest of the Hejaz ended more than a thousand years of Hashemite custodianship of Islam's holiest cities — and reshaped the Hajj for the century that followed.
body:
• In 1924–25, Abdulaziz ibn Saud's forces seized Mecca, Medina and Jeddah from King Hussein bin Ali's Hashemite kingdom of the Hejaz.
  • The Hashemites, who claim descent from the Prophet Muhammad, had guarded Mecca for more than a thousand years.
  • Abdulaziz was proclaimed King of Hejaz in January 1926; the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932.
  • The conquest gave the House of Saud control of the Hajj — the basis of its religious legitimacy to this day.

A hundred years ago this decade, Islam's two holiest cities changed hands. Mecca and Medina — guarded for more than a millennium by the Hashemites, who claim direct descent from the Prophet Muhammad — were taken by Abdulaziz ibn Saud, the Najdi ruler whose family still reigns over Saudi Arabia. The episode is back in the spotlight thanks to an India Today explainer on the conquest.

The takeover, completed in late 1925, ended the short-lived Hashemite Kingdom of the Hejaz and put Islam's holiest sites under Saudi control — the conquest that made the Saudi state possible.

Context & Background

The Hashemites had dominated Mecca for over a thousand years when their position collapsed after World War I, according to GlobalSecurity. Hussein bin Ali, the Sharif of Mecca, had led the 1916 Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire and ruled the Hejaz as king — his family's claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad underpinning their authority over the holy cities.

Their challenger came from the central Arabian region of Najd. Abdulaziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh in 1902 and spent the next two decades consolidating power across the peninsula, according to the Columbia Encyclopedia. The Wahhabi movement, allied with the Saud family since the 18th century, supplied the fervor behind his expansion.

The turning point came in 1924: that March, Turkey abolished the Ottoman caliphate, and Hussein's declaration of himself as caliph won him little support. In September 1924, Saudi forces took the Hejaz city of Taif, and on October 6, Hussein fled Mecca for the Red Sea port of Jeddah, abdicating in favor of his son Ali bin Hussein. Abdulaziz entered Mecca in December 1924 — according to Saudipedia, he arrived in the pilgrim's state of ihram to perform Umrah.

Britain, which had backed Hussein during the war, stayed on the sidelines. The British did not encourage the Saudi advance on Mecca and Medina, but gave no sign they would oppose it, When Hussein's position collapsed, the British transported him first to Aqaba and then into exile in Cyprus.

Impact & Analysis

With Mecca secured, Saudi forces laid siege to Jeddah, where Ali and the last Hejazi forces held out. The siege began in January 1925 and lasted nearly a year, ending on December 16, 1925, when Ali surrendered under British mediation and left for Baghdad. Medina came under Saudi control peacefully in December 1925, and the settlement was formalized in the Jeddah Agreement of 1925.

In January 1926, Abdulaziz was proclaimed King of the Hejaz — he was already Sultan of Najd — and in 1932 he founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. More than a thousand years of Hashemite rule in Mecca came to an end, according to GlobalSecurity.

"guarantee the liberty of pilgrimage and to settle the destiny of the Holy Land in a manner satisfactory to the Islamic world"

— Abdulaziz ibn Saud, on the invasion of the Hejaz

The new ruler moved quickly to legitimize his custodianship. In 1926 he convened Muslim delegations in Mecca and introduced them to his religious establishment, according to historian Frank Smitha's account; pilgrimages became regular and grew in size. Abdulaziz also took the title Khadim al Haramayn — Servant of the Two Holy Shrines — assuming what GlobalSecurity describes as an important position in the wider Muslim world.

The Hashemites did not disappear: Hussein's son Faisal became king of Iraq, and his son Abdullah became emir — later king — of Transjordan, founding the dynasty that still rules Jordan.

Diaspora Angle

For the millions of Muslims who travel for Hajj and Umrah each year — including the large diaspora communities across India, the Gulf, Britain and North America — the 1924–25 conquest is the hinge of modern pilgrimage administration. The Saudi state that emerged runs the quotas, visas and logistics for the holy cities — and the monarchy's claim to religious legitimacy.

Looking Ahead

A century on, the questions raised by the takeover linger. Custodianship of Mecca and Medina remains a subject of debate across the Muslim world — from the Saudi management of the Hajj to the destruction of historic sites around the holy cities under Wahhabi doctrine. Whatever one's view, the record is clear: the House of Saud holds Islam's holiest cities today not by inheritance, but by conquest.
